title: Air Conditioning
summary: Car air conditioning does not make cold — it moves heat out of the cabin. Follow refrigerant around the compressor, condenser, expansion valve and evaporator, and learn why the same system clears a misted windscreen in winter.

seo.title: How Car Air Conditioning Works: The AC Cycle
seo.description: How car air conditioning moves heat out of the cabin: refrigerant, compressor, condenser, expansion valve and evaporator, and why AC also dries the air.

learningObjectives: Identify the high- and low-pressure sides of the system
Explain why air conditioning dries air and helps demist the windscreen
Describe how electric vehicles use electric compressors and heat pumps
beginnerExplanation:
When a liquid evaporates it absorbs heat — that is why you feel cold stepping out of a swimming pool. Air conditioning uses this effect in a closed loop. A special fluid called refrigerant evaporates inside a small radiator behind the dashboard (the evaporator), soaking up heat from the air blown over it, so cooler air reaches the cabin.

The heat then has to be dumped outside. A compressor, driven by the engine or an electric motor, squeezes the refrigerant vapour, which makes it hot. It flows to another radiator at the front of the car (the condenser), where outside air cools it until it turns back into liquid. Finally it passes through a tiny restriction that drops its pressure, making it cold again, ready to absorb more heat in the cabin.

Cooling air below its dew point makes moisture condense on the evaporator, which drains out under the car. That is why air conditioning also dries the air — and why switching it on, even with the heater set to warm, clears a misted windscreen so quickly.
technicalExplanation:
The system runs a vapour-compression cycle with refrigerant R-1234yf in most new cars (older vehicles use R-134a, which has a much higher global-warming potential). The compressor raises low-pressure vapour (roughly 2–3 bar gauge in operation) to high pressure (roughly 10–20 bar depending on ambient temperature), and its temperature rises with it. Engine-driven compressors are swash-plate types, either cycled by an electromagnetic clutch or with internally controlled variable displacement; electric and hybrid vehicles use high-voltage scroll compressors independent of engine speed.

In the condenser the superheated vapour rejects heat to ambient air, condenses and is often subcooled. A receiver-drier (with a thermostatic expansion valve) or an accumulator (with a fixed orifice tube) stores liquid and removes moisture, which would otherwise freeze at the expansion device or form acids. The expansion device throttles the liquid to low pressure: it flashes partly to vapour and its saturation temperature falls to just above 0 °C. In the evaporator it boils, absorbing latent heat from the cabin air; the expansion valve modulates flow to keep a small superheat at the evaporator outlet so only vapour returns to the compressor. An evaporator temperature sensor prevents icing.

Efficiency is expressed as coefficient of performance, COP = Q̇_evaporator / W_compressor, typically around 2–3 for car systems: 1 kW of compressor work moves 2–3 kW of heat. The HVAC module mixes air from the evaporator and the heater core via blend doors, so the evaporator can dehumidify while the heater re-warms the air. Many electric vehicles reverse the cycle as a heat pump, extracting heat from outside air or drivetrain coolant to warm the cabin at a COP above 1, which significantly reduces the range penalty of winter heating compared with resistive heaters.

steps.title: Compress the vapour
steps.beginner: The compressor squeezes refrigerant gas, making it hot and high-pressure.
steps.technical: Low-side vapour (≈ 2–3 bar) is compressed to ≈ 10–20 bar; discharge temperature rises well above ambient.

steps.title: Reject heat outside
steps.beginner: In the condenser at the front of the car, outside air cools the gas until it turns into liquid.
steps.technical: Desuperheating, condensation and subcooling in the condenser reject cabin heat plus compressor work to ambient.

steps.title: Drop the pressure
steps.beginner: A tiny valve lets the liquid through into a low-pressure area, where it becomes very cold.
steps.technical: A TXV or orifice tube throttles the liquid; flash evaporation lowers its saturation temperature to near 0 °C.

steps.title: Absorb cabin heat
steps.beginner: The cold refrigerant boils in the evaporator, taking heat out of the air blown into the cabin.
steps.technical: Latent heat of vaporisation absorbs Q̇_evap; the TXV maintains a few kelvin of superheat at the outlet.

steps.title: Dry the air
steps.beginner: Moisture condenses on the cold evaporator and drains away, so the air leaving it is dry.
steps.technical: Air cooled below its dew point sheds water; reheating it through the heater core produces warm, dry air for demisting.

keyConcepts.definition: Heat absorbed or released when a substance changes phase without changing temperature; evaporation absorbs it.
Heat moved divided by work input; car A/C systems typically achieve around 2–3.
The temperature at which air becomes saturated and water vapour starts to condense.
A refrigeration cycle run to deliver heat into the cabin, moving more heat than the electrical energy it consumes.

misconceptions.reality: It moves heat from the cabin to the outside air. That is why the condenser at the front gets hot while the system runs.
It is the fastest way to dry cabin air and clear misting in cold, damp weather, and running it periodically keeps compressor seals lubricated.

misconceptions.myth: A system that blows warm air just needs a top-up.
misconceptions.reality: Refrigerant does not get used up; a low charge means a leak. Simply recharging without fixing the leak releases more refrigerant to the atmosphere.

practicalExamples: A puddle of clear water under the car on a hot day is condensate from the evaporator, not a leak.
Setting the heater to warm with A/C on clears a fogged windscreen faster than heat alone, because the air is dried first.
On older engine-driven systems you may feel a slight dip in idle speed as the compressor clutch engages.

quiz.prompt: Where does the heat removed from the cabin end up?
options: It is destroyed by the refrigerant
It is released to outside air at the condenser
It is stored in the battery
It goes into the engine oil
quiz.explanation: The condenser rejects the cabin heat, plus the compressor's work, to the air flowing through the front of the car.

quiz.prompt: A compressor uses 1.5 kW and the system's COP is 2.4. How much heat is removed from the cabin?
Why does switching on the A/C help clear a misted windscreen in winter?
options: It dries the air by condensing moisture on the evaporator
It adds fresh refrigerant to the air
quiz.explanation: Cooling air below its dew point removes water; the heater can then re-warm that dry air.

faq.question: How does car air conditioning work?
faq.answer: A compressor pumps refrigerant around a closed loop. In the evaporator behind the dashboard the refrigerant boils at low pressure and absorbs heat from the cabin air; the compressor then raises its pressure and temperature, and the condenser at the front of the car releases that heat outside.

faq.question: Why does car AC help demist the windscreen?
faq.answer: Air passing over the cold evaporator drops below its dew point, so its moisture condenses out and drains away. The drier air, even when reheated, clears misted glass much faster.

faq.question: Does using the air conditioning use more fuel?
faq.answer: Yes. The compressor is driven by the engine, or by the battery in an electric car, so running the AC adds load and uses some extra energy. How much depends on the outside temperature and how hard the system has to work.
